I can't answer the first question, but for the second, font size is
calculated from the base_size parameter which is a theme parameter.

Compare:
qplot(mpg, data=mtcars)
to
qplot(mpg, data=mtcars) + theme_grey(base_size=30)

There are probably better ways to set the theme parameters, using
theme_update(), but this way worked for me.

Font sizes can also be individually modified, according to the ggplot2
book.

Bob

I'm not sure what you mean by writing the labels upside down, but you can rotate the text 90 degrees and make the font bigger with this:
  opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(angle=90, hjust=1.2, size=16))
The hjust=1.2 shifts the text to the left (after rotation) so that it doesn't go into the plotting area.

In general, you can use opts() and theme_text() to change font sizes.

This will display  properties which can be set with opts():
  theme_gray()

And this will tell you how to use theme_text:

messages.body_plain:
Winston's ideas work should work nicely.  To fix the long strings, you can put "\n" in the character strings used in the label (it is interpreted just as if it were given to cat).  Here's an example :

d <- diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds),10),]
qplot(cut, data = d, geom = 'bar') +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = rep('thisiswaytoo\nlooooooong',5)) +
  opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1))

As for Winston's question regarding the use of base_size, here's how it works.  theme_gray creates a list whose elements are (for the most part) functions, such as theme_text, theme_line, etc .  Those functions require parameters which are defined in reference to the parent function's environment (i.e., theme_gray's environment) which is defined when the function itself is defined (base_size is a parameter of theme_gray, it defaults to 12).  That is to say that within the function theme_gray a variable named base_size exists; so, when subsequent functions are defined within theme_gray's environment, they are defined in reference to that variable which exists there, by that name, already having been set.  Since they don't exist outside that environment, you can't refer to them as in, for example, opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(base_size*2)).  Here is a similar example

rm(f,a)
f <- function(a = 5){
  function(x) a * x
}
value <- f()
value
value(2)
a + 7
a <- 20
value(2)

I hope it helps!!

Cheers
david.

On Fri, Jun 26, 2009 at 12:41 PM, Peter
Flom<peterflom...@mindspring.com> wrote:
> The whole question gets interesting.

> How much of the lines are what Tufte would call 'chartjunk'?  I am sure Tufte would
> prefer that graphs contain a lot fewer gridlines than most ggplot graphs contain.  I am
> also sure that I think Tufte goes too far .... his aesthetic purity of "bits of info per square inch"
> sacrifices some clarity.  It's not how much info you can cram onto a page, it's how much the reader
> can get out, and how easily.

I agree.  See the following paper for an example of why you shouldn't
accept Tufte's advice uncritically:

W. A. Stock and J. T. Behrens. Box, line, and midgap plots: Effects of
display characteristics on the accuracy and bias of estimates of
whisker length. Journal of Educational Statistics, 16(1): 1–20, 1991.

And section 3 of the following paper gives some concrete reasons why
you actually want grid lines:

W. Cleveland. A model for studying display methods of statistical
graphics. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics, 2:
323–364, 1993. URL http://stat.bell-labs.com/doc/93.4.ps.

> But how did Hadley decide on the number of grid lines?
>
> How do we adjust it?

They just match up to the tick on the x axis.

> width to disguise points between the quartiles and the

> p<-ggplot(mtcars,aes(factor(cyl),mpg))
> print(p+geom_boxplot(aes(fill=cyl,colour=cyl,size=1.9))+geom_point(aes
> (colour=mtcars$cyl))+stat_summary
> (fun.y=median,geom="crossbar",ymin=0,ymax=0,color="grey90"))

A couple of small fixes:

ggplot(mtcars, aes(factor(cyl), mpg)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = cyl, colour = cyl), size = 1.9) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = cyl))+
  stat_summary(fun.y = median, geom = "crossbar", ymin = 0, ymax = 0,
color = "grey90")

 * when you set the size (rather than mapping it to a variable), it
should be outside of aes
 * you shouldn't use the dataset name in the aesthetic specification
 * it'seasiertoreadwithspaces ;)

> I tried to apply this same idea to my dataset, but can't
> seem to get the groups right (I just get the median by
> factor), nor can I see how to color the outliers
> (they're still black).  Here's one attempt with these
> problems.
> bpl <- ggplot(b, aes(factor(j), i))
> print(bpl +
>      geom_boxplot(aes(fill=k,colour=k,size=1.9)) +
>      stat_summary
> (fun.y=median,geom="crossbar",ymin=-1.0,ymax=1.0,color="grey90"))

If you're going to take this approach, it's much easier to work with
facetting, rather than dodging:

ggplot(b, aes(k, i)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = k, colour = k), size = 1.9) +
  stat_summary(fun.y = median, fun.ymax = median, fun.ymin = median,
    geom = "crossbar", color = "grey90") + facet_grid(. ~ j)

(also note how I set the minimum and maximum values of the crossbar to
the median - a bit of a hack but it works)

Getting the outliers on the plot is a bit more tricky.  The best way
is just to calculate them yourself:

out <- ddply(b, c("j", "k"), function(df) {
  data.frame(i = boxplot.stats(df$i)$out)
})

ggplot(b, aes(k, i, fill = k, colour = k)) +
  geom_boxplot(size = 1.9, outlier.colour = NA) +
  stat_summary(fun.y = median, fun.ymax = median, fun.ymin = median,
    geom = "crossbar", color = "grey90") +
  geom_point(data = out) +
  facet_grid(. ~ j)

messages.body_plain:
> As for Winston's question regarding the use of base_size, here's how it works.  theme_gray creates a list whose elements are (for the most part) functions, such as theme_text, theme_line, etc .  Those functions require parameters which are defined in reference to the parent function's environment (i.e., theme_gray's environment) which is defined when the function itself is defined (base_size is a parameter of theme_gray, it defaults to 12).  That is to say that within the function theme_gray a variable named base_size exists; so, when subsequent functions are defined within theme_gray's environment, they are defined in reference to that variable which exists there, by that name, already having been set.  Since they don't exist outside that environment, you can't refer to them as in, for example, opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(base_size*2)).  Here is a similar example
>
> rm(f,a)
> f <- function(a = 5){
>   function(x) a * x
> }
> value <- f()
> value
> value(2)
> a + 7
> a <- 20
> value(2)

I understand that, in general, you can't refer from outside the environment to a variable that exists inside the environment. But (to me), it looks like the themes themselves allow for references to variables. I'm probably not saying this clearly, so here's an illustration of the issue:

- First, set the theme to theme_gray and then look at axis.text.x and axis.text.y:

theme_set(theme_gray())

theme_get()$axis.text.x
# theme_text(colour = "grey50", size = base_size * 0.8, vjust = 1,
#     lineheight = 0.9)

theme_get()$axis.text.y
# theme_text(colour = "grey50", size = base_size * 0.8, hjust = 1,
#     lineheight = 0.9)

- Now we'll change axis.text.x to use a bigger font, still referring to base_size:

theme_update(axis.text.x = theme_text(colour = "grey50", size = base_size * 2, hjust = 1, lineheight = 0.9))
# no complaints

theme_get()$axis.text.x
# theme_text(colour = "grey50", size = base_size * 2, hjust = 1,
#     lineheight = 0.9)

theme_get()$axis.text.y
# theme_text(colour = "grey50", size = base_size * 0.8, hjust = 1,
#     lineheight = 0.9)

- At this point, it looks like axis.text.x has been successfully set -- it appears to reference base_size in the same way as axis.text.y. But if you try to actually plot something, it complains:

qplot(mpg, data=mtcars)
# Error in inherits(x, "factor") : object "base_size" not found

If they refer to base_size in the same way, why does this happen?
And if they don't refer to base_size in the same way, why does it look like they do?

Also, David, what are you using for the syntax highlighting in your email? I like it.

-Winston

They don't refer to base_size in the same way - they just look like
they do.  I used a quick hack to generate the printed version of the
theme elements - it just shows you the call used to create the
element, which most of the time is exactly what you want.  In this
case it's a bit confusing because it refers to a variable that doesn't
exist in the global namespace.  The reason you don't see the error
right away is because the functions are "lazy", and put off having to
do any work until they absolutely have to - i.e. when they actually
need to draw the element they discover they don't know what base_size
is.

Does that make sense?

Because you are not supplying an overall data frame in the ggplot()

ggplot(mapping = aes(date, value)) +
  geom_line(data = upper) +
  geom_area(data = lower) +

  facet_wrap(~ position, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_date()

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The general idea is to create a grid.layout of viewports using Grid,
then print the plots using the vp argument. AFAIK it should be the
same procedure for all devices. Perhaps the following function can
inspire you,

vp.layout =
function (x, y)
viewport(layout.pos.row = x, layout.pos.col = y)

arrange =
function (..., nrow = NULL, ncol = NULL, as.table = F)
{
    dots <- list(...)
    n <- length(dots)
    if (is.null(nrow) & is.null(ncol)) {
        nrow = floor(n/2)
        ncol = ceiling(n/nrow)
    }
    if (is.null(nrow)) {
        nrow = ceiling(n/ncol)
    }
    if (is.null(ncol)) {
        ncol = ceiling(n/nrow)
    }
    grid.newpage()
    pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(nrow, ncol)))
    ii.p <- 1
    for (ii.row in seq(1, nrow)) {
        ii.table.row <- ii.row
        if (as.table) {
            ii.table.row <- nrow - ii.table.row + 1
        }
        for (ii.col in seq(1, ncol)) {
            ii.table <- ii.p
            if (ii.p > n)
                break
            print(dots[[ii.table]], vp = vp.layout(ii.table.row,
                ii.col))
            ii.p <- ii.p + 1
        }
    }
}

p1 = qplot(1,1)
p2 = qplot(1:10,1:10)

arrange(p1, p2) # interactive use (tested on quartz())

pdf()
arrange(p1,p2, ncol=1) # you'll need to define a more general way
# to specify the positions and dimensions
dev.off()

in that case you'll need to provide the user with a way to specify the
position and size of each viewport. For instance, (click twice on an
interactive device)

p1 = qplot(1,1)
p2 = qplot(1:10,1:10)

# size of the viewports in native units
widths = c(0.5, 0.2)
heights = c(0.3, 0.3)

grid.newpage()
l1 = grid.locator() # click on the page where you want your first plot
vp1 = viewport(x=l1$x, y= l1$y, width= widths[1], height=heights[1])
print(p1, vp = vp1)
l2 = grid.locator()# click on the page where you want your second plot
vp2 = viewport(x=l2$x, y= l2$y, width= widths[2], height=heights[2])
print(p2, vp = vp2)

And of course you may replace grid.locator() with previously defined
coordinates. A trickier part might be for you to place the viewports
so that they use the available nicely. Grid provides some utilities
that might help you (grid.pack etc.).

messages.subject: Hybrid continuous/discrete faceted axes
messages.body_plain:
I work in genetics, and have been making plots using ggplot2 that plot
association values or expression levels on the y-axis with genetic
position on the x axis.

I have been struggling for a while on how to annotate these plots with
information that also varies along the x-axis, such as the location of
genes, SNPs, etc.

It seemed to me that the "correct" way to do this would be to use a
shared x-axis, since all the various data I am plotting has this in
common, and the supported way to do that in ggplot2, as far as I can
tell, is to use faceting.  I was able to use facet_grid to show two
different continuous  variables, but when I tried to also show data
that has no continuous y-component but rather is categorical (such as
gene tracks), this resulted in various error messages (even when using
scales="free") and didn't work.

I can see how it might be difficult to implement this on the back-end,
but do you think it is a capability that might make sense to add?  It
seems to me that it would be very useful to allow the concept of
"scale freedom" to extend beyond just having different limits on the
continuous scales to allow them to include discrete data as well.
Much of the annotation data we want to present alongside our results
looks like this, at least in my field, and it is very helpful to have
this annotation data presented in the same plot as, e.g. association
data, in order to better interpret the results.

In the meantime, I've had to kludge it by making up continuous values
for each discrete value and plotting them in the negative portion of
the y-axis, but having to do that breaks all kinds of things when it
comes to separating the data from the presentation, so it would be
really nice if some way to do this were supported within ggplot2.

An example of the sort of data I am working with is:
http://www.broadinstitute.org/files/shared/diabetes/scandinavs/chr9.jpg

Though in those plots they have also used two different continuous y-
axes in the same region of the plot, which I am now mostly convinced
is a bad idea because it is hard for the person viewing them not to
unintentionally compare the relative position of elements drawn on the
two different scales.  In this case, that data can easily be displayed
using faceting in ggplot2 (with a free y-axis). The issue is the gene
track at the bottom that shows the location and direction of the genes
-- I can't find a clean way to present that information using ggplot2.

messages.subject_clean: two questions about stat_smooth and glm
messages.body_plain:
I have two quick questions about plotting the results of a glm
analysis using ggplot2.

Let us assume I have data that the x value varies from 0 to 1, has
some noise, and then is exponentiated.  This leads to a gamma type of
error.  Assume there is also some error in measurement, leading to the
occasional negative measurement and such.  I wish to then plot both
the data and a curve fitted using a generalized linear model with a
Gamma error and a log link.

Now, two questions

1) Is there a way to plot the curve of interest, but ONLY plot it for
groups (and I'm using facets here) for which you get a result that
meets some criterion (e.g. where the coefficient p value < 0.05 in my
case).

2)Due to negative values from measurement error, one needs to add a
slight offset to the y values for the fit.  How can one do this and
still get a properly plotted line.  Currently I'm getting "Error in
eval(expr, envir, enclos) :
   non-positive values not allowed for the gamma family" errors
regardless of different attempts to add offsets with  the formula in
stat_smooth.

Here is some sample code I have been playing with for this problem.

#create data - x is a predictor, g is a group, y is the response
x<-seq(0,1,.01)

g<-as.factor(c("A", "B", "C", "D"))
z<-data.frame(expand.grid(x=x,g=g))

#add a little error in to our results
set.seed(1001)
z$y<- rnorm(length(z$x), z$x*c(.3,1.5,2.9, 5.0)[unclass(z$g)], sd=0.1)
z$y=rnorm(length(z$x), exp(z$y), sd=2)

#this first bit just sets up the basic plotting, with colors and panels
a<-qplot(x,y,group=g, colour=g, data=z)+facet_wrap( ~ g, scales="free")

#now, add a fitted line with the error around it shown.
a+stat_smooth(method="glm", se=T, group=g, fill="black",
family=Gamma(link="log"), formula=(y+1)~x)

Thanks!

-Jarrett

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jarrett,

It sounds like you're trying to do something that's a bit too
complicated for stat_smooth.  I'd suggest fitting the models
separately, and predicting on a grid of x values and then plotting the
predictions in a separate layer:

# Fit model to each group.  I'm just using a linear model here because I
# know how to extract the overall model p-value.
models <- dlply(z, "g", function(df) lm(y ~ x, data = df))

# Calculate pvalue
pvalues <- laply(models, function(mod) {
  fstat <- summary(mod)$fstatistic
  pf(fstat[1L], fstat[2L], fstat[3L], lower.tail = FALSE)
})

# Only look at significant models
signif <- models[pvalues < 0.05]

# Create grid and add predictions
grid <- data.frame(x = seq(0, 1, length = 20))
predictions <- ldply(signif, function(model) {
  grid$y <- predict(model, newdata = grid)
  grid
})
# Shouldn't have to do this, but it looks like there's a bug in plyr
names(predictions)[1] <- "g"

qplot(x, y, colour = g, data = z) +
  facet_wrap(~ g, scales="free") +
  geom_line(data = predictions)

However, off the top of my head, I don't know how to resolve your
problem with negative values.  Simply adding a offset is unlikely to
be the right solution.

Hadley

messages.body_plain:
Hadley,

Thanks for consdering it -- I suspected it would not be an easy change
to add this to the faceting, though I do think that many users might
find it very useful (it certainly comes up in a large percentage of
the plots that I do).  I agree that a hybrid scale would probably be
an easier way to solve it, but I see what you mean about not having a
data type in which you can put a mixed vector or factor/numeric types,
and I guess there probably isn't a lot of use for it in general.

Another way to solve the "problem" (in a less kludgey way than making
up fake continuous values for each of my discrete categories) would be
to make it easier to align scales across ggplot2 plots printed into
different viewports (basically making it possible to do "manual"
faceting).

This is already (sort of) possible by turning extra legends off and
forcing the scale limits to be the same, but it seems like there could
be a way to create an interface to make this easier, to make it work
even when there are extra elements (such as legends) in the margins.
I guess the problem with this is probably that the scale isn't
actually mapped to grid units until the plot is actually drawn, and
that data is (I am guessing) only contained in the grid objects.

Perhaps if we could create a new option for the scale functions that
would allow you to specify an existing ggplot2 viewport from which it
will copy all of its settings?  Does that seem like something that
might be a bit easier to add?  Is the necessary data currently stored
in the grid objects?

Josh.

p2 = p %+% mpg2

pdf()

print(p2)
dev.off()

messages.subject: Re: Facet labels
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I think plotmath isn't currently supported for facet labels. You can
try these two options and see if it works for you,

# first option: use UTF8 characters (may depend on your machine and device)
f = sample(letters[1:2],10, repl=T)
labels = paste(c(17,14),"º")

d = data.frame(x=1:10,y=rnorm(10),f=factor(f, labels= labels))
str(d)

library(ggplot2)
p =
qplot(x,y, data= d) + facet_grid(. ~ f)

# second option: use latex and the new tikzDevice package
d1 = data.frame(x=1:10,y=rnorm(10),f=factor(f,
labels=c("$14^{\\circ}$","$17^{\\circ}$")))

p1 =
qplot(x,y, data= d1) + facet_grid(. ~ f)

#p1

library(tikzDevice)

tikz("test.tex", standAlone =T)
print(p1)
dev.off()

system("/usr/texbin/pdflatex test.tex",int=T)
system("open test.pdf")

Alternatively you might be able to locate the grob.texts corresponding
to the facet labels in the ggplot gTree, in which case you could use
